questions.q: What are the five parts of the presentation structure this lesson recommends, in order?
options: Context and requirements; high-level architecture; deep dives on load-bearing decisions; tradeoffs and risks; close and roadmap
High-level architecture; context; Q&A; tradeoffs; close
Deep dives; tradeoffs; context; roadmap; high-level architecture
Close and roadmap; context; deep dives; high-level architecture; tradeoffs
questions.explain: The structure runs context/requirements, high-level architecture, deep dives on load-bearing decisions, tradeoffs and risks, then close and roadmap -- each section builds on the shared understanding the previous one established.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why is a pre-planned time budget useful even though the goal isn't clock-watching during the live presentation?
options: Because reciting exact minutes out loud impresses the board
Because without a budget the opening tends to run long and the close -- where the recommendation gets planted -- gets rushed or cut, which is backwards
Because review boards require a printed time budget as a scoring artifact
Time budgets have no real effect on how a presentation actually unfolds
questions.explain: A presentation with no time plan tends to drift, spending too long on the comfortable opening and running out of time for the close -- exactly backwards, since the close is what the board walks away remembering. The budget is a rehearsal planning tool, not a live script.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say giving every component equal depth is the single most common structural mistake?
options: Because it is technically impossible to present multiple components at equal depth
Because it wastes limited attention on decisions that don't actually drive the rest of the design, and signals the presenter can't distinguish load-bearing decisions from incidental ones
Because boards only ever ask about the first component presented
Because equal depth makes a presentation too short
questions.explain: A board has limited time and will remember only a few things -- spending that attention equally across load-bearing and incidental decisions wastes it, and signals to the board that the presenter doesn't know which decisions actually matter most.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend naming your own design's tradeoffs and risks before the board asks about them?
options: Because every real design has tradeoffs, and proactively naming them demonstrates you understand your own design's limits -- a credibility signal an experienced board weighs heavily
Because boards are not allowed to ask about tradeoffs the presenter didn't mention first
Because naming a weakness guarantees the board will overlook it entirely
Because a design with no weaknesses is normal and expected, so tradeoffs are optional to mention
questions.explain: A presentation implying the design has no weaknesses isn't credible to a panel that has reviewed many designs. Naming real tradeoffs proactively signals genuine understanding of the design's limits and removes a line of questioning aimed at testing whether you'd admit weakness under pressure.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what makes a close effective at 'setting up Q&A' rather than just ending the presentation?
options: Trailing off into new content that should have been covered earlier
Restating the recommendation in one sentence, naming what you'd want to validate further, and stopping deliberately rather than running out of material
Ending with a generic phrase like 'that's my design' and waiting for questions
Repeating the entire deep-dive section a second time
questions.explain: A strong close restates the recommendation, names the specific things worth validating further (which often preempts the exact questions coming next), and stops on its own terms -- rather than ending vaguely or by simply running out of prepared content.
